title: Can AI Finally Create Intelligently Varied Practice?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton reports that after years of testing, he thinks a recent Claude model can finally produce intelligently varied practice, the one resource type AI had never done well. He traces the idea to his VariationTheory.com site and the sequences of questions where one critical feature changes at a time, and explains that earlier LLMs changed things arbitrarily, so students missed the connections the sequences are meant to reveal. His method was to give Claude examples and non-examples, explain how he builds sequences from skills, critical features and misconceptions, and then iterate by challenging its decisions. Claude suggested multiple chains of examples ending in mixed practice, and the result is a new resource type he calls Minimally Different Mega Practice, with a full-screen present mode for projecting the previous question. He suggests using the sequences for consolidation and method selection, with a 4-2 working routine or the reflect-expect-check-explain model.
points: Earlier LLMs failed at varied practice because their changes between questions were arbitrary, so students never noticed the critical feature the sequence was meant to isolate.
Barton prepared the model by sharing good and bad example sequences, explaining his planning process, and asking Claude to restate it before building anything.
Using several short chains of examples, each ending in mixed practice, removes the pressure of getting a single first example exactly right.
Once one build is right it becomes a template, so each success improves every later resource through accumulated examples and principles.
The sequences suit mixed-topic consolidation and method selection, and can be run with a silent four-minute, discuss-two-minute routine or with reflect, expect, check and explain prompts.
quotes: However, the results were underwhelming, to say the least. Sure, the LLMs could change one thing, but they did so arbitrarily. When changes are arbitrary, students miss critical features, connections aren't made, and the deeper understanding, surprise, and thinking these sequences are meant to engender simply doesn’t happen.

I first shared examples and non-examples of what I wanted to create. I chose some of my favourite sequences from my variation theory website (created by myself or by some of the wonderful teachers who’ve shared their sequences over the years), and some not-so-good sequences, including ones I’ve created myself and early attempts by LLMs.

Getting that first example right is crucial because all other examples stem from it as minimal changes. Claude suggested that, instead of tying everything to a single chain, I could use multiple chains of examples throughout a resource.

When building resources with AI, once you have one example you’re happy with, you’re laughing because that can become a template for all examples that follow. Each successful build improves all future builds, as you can teach Claude examples and non-examples, principles, features, things to avoid, and things to strive for.
When I used to write these sequences by hand, the fun bit was always creating the sequence on a scrap of paper. The painful bit was then writing it up in a nice-looking worksheet or PowerPoint.
This is great mixed-topic consolidation practice because students have to focus and pay attention to what has changed and how that affects the outcome.

I like students to work through these activities using my 4-2 approach: students work in silence for 4 minutes, then have 2 minutes to discuss how far they’ve got and check their answers with a partner.
